Contrastive and self‑supervised learning have become central to graph‑based recommender systems because they can generate auxiliary training signals without requiring additional labels. Early graph collaborative‑filtering models already incorporated contrastive objectives to mitigate data sparsity, but they typically relied on random sampling of negative pairs and ignored the relational structure among neighboring users or items, limiting their effectiveness [S2:3fe92dae73a1d98a52a73c1c46a5be3dafd0c14d]. Subsequent work explicitly addressed sparsity and noisy feedback by designing robust graph contrastive frameworks that jointly model the interaction graph and its perturbations, thereby improving recommendation accuracy under sparse and noisy conditions [S2:90eed4e1cc8f13a8ece64328cd8219e06c13d0e9]. However, many of these methods still depend on costly graph‑convolution operations to produce augmented views, which raises computational overhead and hampers scalability [S2:dd511e6bb0cc427384f4bf8499dedac428f35e3f].

A major line of research has focused on how to construct high‑quality contrastive views. Structure‑augmentation approaches modify the topology of the user‑item graph while preserving semantic consistency, and attribute‑aware schemes enrich the augmentations with node features to compensate for weak interaction signals [S2:b6e8b6d09e90c728885693fd9f32d6a6593306a5]. Recognizing that naïve perturbations (e.g., random edge dropout) can produce “noisy views” that share little information with the original graph, symmetric graph contrastive learning has been proposed to explicitly filter out such detrimental augmentations and enforce bidirectional consistency [S2:9938b457cc72003b1b691c9da825d4a30734a2b1]. In parallel, simplified contrastive objectives that directly optimize alignment and uniformity have shown that elaborate augmentations are not always necessary; instead, aligning embeddings of the same node across views while dispersing different nodes can achieve competitive performance with reduced complexity [S2:2453ed89166b6a6f4765bd07cfe83fcac041ac37].

Beyond view generation, recent studies have enriched the contrastive paradigm with richer learning signals. Simultaneously leveraging local (node‑level) and global (graph‑level) contrastive objectives enables the model to capture fine‑grained preferences as well as holistic user behavior patterns [S2:dd7944eed93a9636f4cbce7ac68125f2bbdabd92]. Counterfactual intervention techniques further enhance graph contrastive learning by explicitly modeling missing‑not‑at‑random biases inherent in implicit feedback, thereby correcting for data bias and improving recommendation robustness [S2:ade0b7f79e5cdeee4f6d4f23e4f97f382b786d34]. In domains where false negatives are prevalent—such as academic reviewer recommendation—negative‑sampling‑enhanced contrastive learning mitigates the assumption that unobserved edges are truly negative, leading to more reliable recommendations [S2:a280deb68d656acbdf28adb82ccfdddac1d8886f]. Moreover, extending contrastive learning to multi‑behavior settings allows the integration of diverse interaction types (e.g., clicks, purchases, likes) within a unified framework, further boosting recommendation quality [S2:4e1e1cc795d3ec3ff51c9b28bc1d9e6c7f09662f].

Overall, the literature converges on three complementary trends: (1) designing efficient, information‑preserving augmentations that avoid noisy views; (2) formulating contrastive objectives that balance alignment, uniformity, and hierarchical (local‑global) relationships; and (3) incorporating domain‑specific interventions such as counterfactual reasoning or refined negative sampling to address bias and false‑negative issues. Adaptive‑fusion self‑supervised models epitomize this direction by dynamically weighting multiple self‑supervised signals, achieving state‑of‑the‑art performance while curbing the computational burden of traditional augmentation pipelines [S2:dd511e6bb0cc427384f4bf8499dedac428f35e3f][S2:2453ed89166b6a6f4765bd07cfe83fcac041ac37].
